item.title: Eagles News: Cowboys fans jealous of Philadelphia stockpiling draft picks
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles news and links for 11/12/26.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

Even in a season where the Eagles are 2-7 and worse than the Cowboys, Dallas fans still wish their team could be more like the Birds. It’s delicious to see how fans of Philadelphia’s NFC East rivals know that the Eagles won’t be down for long.

Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

The Eagles Have a Plan. The Cowboys Have Jerry Jones. – Blogging The Boys

The Eagles are having a down year, and Howie Roseman is doing what smart front offices do. He’s looking ahead, making trades and stockpiling draft picks to reload with 7 picks in the first two rounds of 2027 and 2028. Meanwhile, in Dallas, Jerry Jones and company continue to convince themselves they’re just a player or two away from contending. Spoiler alert: They’re not. Yet they’ve traded away valuable future picks to prop up a team that isn’t nearly as competitive as they seem to believe.

NFC East Mixtape VOL. 206: The biggest week yet – NFC East Mixtape

The biggest week of the season is here for the NFC East and it is big because of what is happening on Thursday night! The Washington Commanders are set to take on the New York Giants in a game where the latter is trying to take a firm grip on this thing while the former is trying to save their season. Given the importance of the game Scott Bair and Ed Valentine join RJ Ochoa and Brandon Gowton to discuss the matchup and everything encircling the only division where everyone has won the Super Bowl. Oh, and the Dallas Cowboys are also playing a football game this week. You can see that we have a BRAND NEW NFC East Mixtape YouTube Channel so make sure to subscribe as the show will live here exclusively in video format. AND you can also listen to the show! On Blogging The Boys and/or Bleeding Green Nation podcast feeds as well as the SB Nation NFL Show feed!

Eagles aren’t rebuilding. They’re retooling, with the immense draft capital as the backbone. – BGN

The NFL trade deadline came and went for the Philadelphia Eagles, with the lone move in the days leading up to the deadline being the departure of Jordan Davis. Surprising? Not really, it’s hard to sell players off in the NFL — even for a team with a 2-7 record. It’s even harder to negotiate with a general manager like Howie Roseman, a savant at holding onto his players until he can deal them at the right price. See Davis and Cam Jurgens, the other in-season deal the Eagles made prior to the deadline that some seem to (already) forget about. The Eagles got a 2027 first-round pick, 2027 fifth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick, and 2029 second-round pick for Jurgens and Davis — two players drafted in 2022 that clearly weren’t going to be part of the next era of Eagles football. Philadelphia also gave up a 2027 seventh-round pick in the Jurgens deal, and almost recouped a higher pick if the Arnold Ebiketie deal didn’t fall through. Add in the 2028 first-round pick and 2027 fifth-round pick in the A.J. Brown deal five months ago and the Eagles are set for the future. The Eagles have a massive haul of draft picks coming their way over the next three years in the first three rounds — 13 in total.

Game Review – NYG 19, PHI 11 – Iggles Blitz

My biggest frustration with the game wasn’t the loss, but rather the amount of dumb mistakes the team made. Riq Woolen had a block in the back penalty on a punt return. It was blatantly obvious and put the offense in terrible field position. There were a lot of missed blocking assignments in the run and passing games. There was a completely blown coverage in the end zone. Elijah Mitchell had a pair of brain dead moments. I seriously wonder if he understands the game of football. When you are overwhelmed with injuries, the healthy players must play smart football and do the little things rigt to give the team a chance to win. That just isn’t happening with this team.

2026 NFL midseason report: Questions, stats for all 32 teams entering second half – ESPN

Second-half storyline: Can Nick Sirianni save his job? He has built up equity after making the playoffs in each of his first five seasons, complete with a Super Bowl title. But things are a mess, particularly on offense — the side of the ball where his expertise lies. Turnover is coming to the offensive staff. Will Sirianni help oversee the changes, or will he be a part of them?

Eagles midterm grades by position at the bye week in 2026 – NBCSP

It should be no surprise to see the Eagles’ coaching staff gets the worst grade out of everything. This is a poorly coached team right now. The offense is directionless under Sean Mannion, the OL is a wreck under Chris Kuper, the defense has regressed under Vic Fangio and special teams has regressed under Michael Clay. Ultimately, it all falls on Nick Sirianni, who will have to coach for his job the rest of the season. Maybe he gets a mulligan in a season with a bunch of injuries, including one to his starting QB, but there’s a real chance he’s not back for a seventh season in 2027.

2027 NFL Mock Draft: Chargers land Jeremiah Smith, Dolphins find their quarterback in Drew Mestermaker – PFF

5) Philadelphia Eagles: ED Dylan Stewart, South Carolina. Philadelphia’s edge rushers have disappointed this season, and it’s extremely unusual for the team to rank 29th in the NFL in pass-rush grade. Stewart has rebounded from injury to post an elite 90.8 pass-rush grade and an excellent 18% pass-rush win rate. He’s the exact type of high-ceiling rusher the Eagles can develop as they rebuild in the trenches. […] 25) Philadelphia Eagles (via JAX): OT Carter Smith, Indiana. Smith has been Indiana’s starting left tackle for four seasons and continues to play consistently sound football for the Hoosiers. He has allowed just one sack this season after surrendering two in each of the previous three campaigns. Whether he projects as a right tackle or a guard in the NFL, Smith would provide valuable versatility for a Philadelphia team that needs to bolster its offensive line.

NFL Power Rankings, Week 10: Jaguars reach season high; Vikings, Patriots slide after lopsided defeats – NFL.com

31) EAGLES. Philadelphia’s turn to Joe Milton III helped the Eagles hold a temporary lead Sunday before giving it away and losing an ugly game to a division rival. The Eagles’ willingness to trade Jordan Davis to Jacksonville tells us everything we need to know about this team in 2026.

    Zac Taylor offers apology on behalf of Duke Tobin for botched trade with Eagles – Cincy Jungle

    “Obviously, we tried something yesterday. Duke (Tobin) was very explicit with me when he came and spoke to me of how he wanted this portrayed, and I’m not comfortable doing it, but I’m gonna do what he asked,” said Taylor. “We did make an effort to put some depth in there in place of Cashius (Howell). As we got into it, obviously it was going to be a little more costly than we initially anticipated. Duke is really apologetic about it and wants to make clear Philly was a great trade partner and it was on our end, and that’s just the way things go.”

    NY Giants-Washington Commanders not quite ‘for all the marbles’, but it’s big – Big Blue View

    The Giants are 1.5-point favorites to beat the Commanders Thursday night, per FanDuel Sportsbook. The Cowboys host the 7-1 San Francisco 49ers, and Dallas is a 4.5-point underdog. If the Giants win and the Cowboys lose, the NFC East standings will look like this: Giants 6-2-1, Cowboys 4-6, Commanders 2-6-1. The Giants will have a 3½-game lead. In that scenario, if the Giants go a reasonable 3-5 over their final eight games, they would finish 9-7-1. Dallas would have to go 6-1 to get to 10 wins, which is what they would need to win the division since the Giants’ tie with the Commanders counts as half a victory. I doubt even the most ardent of Cowboys fans would feel good about Dallas’s chances of pulling that off.

    7 great NFL rookies are who already changing their teams’ future – SB Nation

    The Browns’ rookie wide receivers, both drafted after Makai Lemon, are also on this list.

    Arvell Reese, LB — New York Giants. Arvell Reese is exactly who we thought he was, and that’s a very good thing for the New York Giants. A do-everything defensive Swiss army knife, Reese has been the biggest x-factor on a Giants defense that is extremely scary, albeit still a work in progress. The rookie has stuffed the stat sheet in almost every area. He has 49 tackles, 4.5 sacks, 32 run stops, 1 forced fumble, and 1 interception. If you need anything on defense, Reese is going to give you it. It feels like we’re not just witnessing the best rookie defender of 2026, but potentially the best defensive player to enter the league since Myles Garrett — that’s how good Arvell Reese has been. Home run pick, and he’s going to run away with the DROY this year.

    Commanders vs. Giants Wednesday injury report: Treylon Burks will play – Hogs Haven

    Commanders receiver Treylon Burks didn’t practice on Wednesday, the last day of prep before Thursday night’s showdown with the New York Giants. That’s not the negative development that it sounds like. That became clear on the official injury report, where Burks was not given a designation. He will play this key upcoming contest, a welcome return after he missed Washington’s loss to the Rams. The Commanders did rule center Lucas Patrick (concussion) and tight end Colson Yankoff (knee) out of this game. No one was considered questionable.

item.title: Week 10 Fantasy Football Sleepers: Puka Nacua injury opens up opportunity for Konata Mumpfield
item.description: Scott Pianowski shares some underrated fantasy football options for your lineup off the waiver wire for Week 10.
item.content:encoded:
DeMario Douglas was the lone hit on the sleeper page last week, while Adonai Mitchell drove us batty (seven targets, tons of air yards, no catches). We’re onto Week 10. Let’s see what undervalued options we can find.

RB Audric Estime vs. Panthers (36%): The status of this sleeper comes down to Travis Etienne Jr.’s status — if Etienne is ready to play again, Estime is too risky to use. But Estime came out of nowhere to post a useful 15-72-1 log last week, and the Panthers have been the second-easiest defense for RBs to score against.

WR Konata Mumpfield at Cardinals (12%): He’s had just one relevant game all year, a 4-93-1 surprise at the Broncos in Week 3. But with Puka Nacua and Davante Adams both hurt, the Rams need some new songs in the passing game; perhaps this is a reasonable spot for Mumpfield and Sons. The Cardinals have been an average matchup for pass production.

RB Dylan Sampson vs. Texans (28%): The Houston defense is parceling out just 3.9 YPC, so it could be another slog for RB Quinshon Judkins. So we’ll leave the light on for Sampson, who has 12 catches the last three weeks and is coming off a season-best 11 touches. Deshaun Watson is also returning, and he steered six passes to Sampson two weeks ago.

QB Aaron Rodgers at Bengals (42%): Hopefully you don’t need a QB streamer this week, though Caleb Williams managers might in a pinch. Rodgers has seen his fantasy score drop in his last three weeks, but he’s rested off the bye and facing a Cincinnati team that could be weary after a Europe trip. Rodgers posted 23 fantasy points when the teams met in Week 3.

RB Kaleb Johnson vs. Vikings (16%): It’s probably a touchdown-or-bust case for Johnson, as the Minnesota defense has been outstanding all year. But solving for volume is most of the puzzle when scouting RBs, and Johnson might be the last back standing in Green Bay, with Josh Jacobs (finger) out and MarShawn Lloyd (knee) uncertain. Johnson was surprisingly useful (14-68-1) at New England last week.

WR Jordan Watkins at Cowboys (5%): Do your injury diligence on this one, as the Niners aren’t sure if Mike Evans or Deebo Samuel Sr. will play this week. If even one of them sits at Dallas, then Watkins could be in play against one of the league’s worst defenses. Watkins had an impressive 4-86-1 breakout against the Raiders last week, including a nifty TD catch on a contested target.

TE Darren Waller at Saints (18%): Maybe you shrugged off his Week 9 breakout, as the Broncos are a TE-funnel defense. But the Saints are the seventh-friendliest defense for TE production, so Waller can help us again. His target share seems to fluctuate weekly, but he always offers touchdown equity (four spikes in eight starts), and that’s what tight-end streaming is usually about.

item.title: Carson Beck "super excited" to make his debut on Sunday
item.description: Cardinals rookie quarterback Carson Beck will make his first start on Sunday against the Rams.
item.content:encoded:
Cardinals rookie quarterback Carson Beck will make his first start on Sunday against the Rams.

Speaking to reporters in a Wednesday press conference, Beck said he’s “super excited” to make his regular-season debut.

“Obviously, having gone from the emergency quarterback at the beginning of the season to last week being the backup to now being the starter, it’s been a crazy season,” Beck said, via transcript from the team. “It’s really been a welcome to the NFL season, just getting introduced to what the league is and what it can be, but I'm super excited for the opportunity and to have the chance to go play with these guys.”

Beck will be the third starting quarterback for the Cardinals this season after Jacoby Brissett and Gardner Minshew. Beck noted he’s picked up plenty from observing both veteran QBs to this point in the year.

“I think the biggest thing is just watching those two and how they carry themselves and how they handle themselves not only in the meeting room around the coaches, but during the walkthrough, during practice, and during the game,” Beck said. “I think that’s the biggest thing that you can learn from those guys, of everybody’s looking at you as a quarterback, and your attitude has to be right each and every day. The moxie [of] going out there, having confidence, and making everyone around you better.

“I think that’s something that I learned in how they carry themselves and when they went on the field — how I need to carry myself as well.”

To that end, Beck said “of course” he can maintain his sense of confidence entering Sunday.

“I think the coolest thing about confidence is that confidence is a choice,” Beck said. "With that also, I’ve said it before, it makes everyone else around you better as well. It exudes confidence into them when you’re showing that you’re confident. When you can choose that, again, you just have to go out there and execute. You have to go out there and do your thing and you have to go out there and be confident, have swag, and have moxie. Regardless of the circumstances, regardless of anything going on around you, regardless of maybe what happened the play before or maybe thinking about what’s going to happen the next play.

“You have to be in the present moment and that’s really all you can do and control.”

item.title: Are the Houston Texans ascending or pretending?
item.description: Houston Texans vs. themselves
item.content:encoded:
Life as a fan of the Houston Texans is all about tempering expectations. They don’t seem to bump along the runway forever, but can’t seem to maintain cruising altitude either. We’ve all seen them light up an opponent one week, then struggle and fall the next. This begs the question: which version of the Texans takes the field against the Cleveland Browns this Sunday?

Do you think this team is about to go on a winning streak that ends in the playoffs? Or, will they pull out the old-reliable jumbo offense, forgot-how-to-tackle defense and let former Texans quarterback Deshawn Watson lead his Brownies to a win?

Vote:

Personally, I think the Browns are going down.

We told you so!

First off, for all the people out there who raged about C.J. Stroud over the off-season. For the ones who called him trash, wanted him gone, swore up and down he was the worst QB on earth: you were so, soooo wrong.

So wrong.

After the absolute clinic he put on last weekend against the Los Angeles Chargers, throwing 35 passes for 21 completions, 384 yards, 125.5 passer rating, 5 touchdowns and only 1 interception, Stroud took home his 2nd AFC Player of the Week honor. He’s now the only player in the league to win it twice this season.

Still not convinced? Think Stroud’s game was a fluke? Doubling down on your silly belief that he isn’t all that? How about this:

Now that we’ve established Stroud is clearly not the problem, let’s take another minute to bask in the glory of it all:

Ok, now that we’ve settled that. Time to look ahead.

Houston Texans vs. Cleveland Browns

The Cleveland Browns are currently 5-4, have the 29th ranked offense, 17th ranked defense and lost a nail biter last weekend to the New Orleans Saints 22-23. At first glance, it seems like this should be a close game, particularly with Watson facing the team that dumped him in Cleveland with no bus fare back to H-Town.

However, the Browns offense doesn’t have the stroke to stop Will Anderson Jr. and 10 of his best friends.

Spencer Fano and (former Texans) Tytus Howard are currently ranked as #1 and #2 worse tackles in the NFL. For every Juice Scruggs who leaves the Nick Caley system to overachieve elsewhere, there’s a Tytus Howard who makes Caserio look like a genius for shedding him as one of the last vestiges of Bill O’Brien’s GM incompetence.

Anderson Jr. is currently the NFL’s leading sack-master, with 9.5 on the season. Browns left tackle Fano has given up 8.5 sacks. Watson was sacked 62 times in his 2018 campaign with the Texans. While a lot of those were poor blocking and bad scheming, quite a few were on Watson for holding the ball too long.

Hold the ball too long this Sunday, with Fano trying to ward off Anderson Jr. as Howard looks to stop Danielle Hunter, Sheldon Rankins and/or Jadeveon Clowney and Watson is going to have a long, long day.

It’s honestly possible for the Texans defense to top last week’s 8 sacks when facing off against the Browns’s tackles. The 8 qb drops ties a team record. Could Deshaun Watson go down (pun intended) in the history books as the most sacked QB in a game vs the Texans? That would certainly feel right. 9 sacks? 10? The front 7 has to be drooling at the prospects…

What might stop the good guys from bringing home another dub? Despite Stroud’s amazing effort last week, the Texans still have no run game and no answer at tailback aside from Woody Marks. They let the trade deadline come and go without landing a starting level running back, which also means Caserio didn’t overpay for one. Rumor has it the Indianapolis Colts were holding their breath for a 1st round draft pick in exchange for Jonathan Taylor. Regardless, the Texans head into Cleveland with a smash mouth run game that lacks the capability to smash any mouths.

Another X-factor is the defense. Did Coach Ryans’ back-to-basics tackling drills help refocus this crew? They held the Chargers to only 9 points through the first 3 quarters. LA only made 14 first downs and converted a measly 5 third downs into firsts. For perspective, the Chargers entered last week’s game with the 32nd ranked offense and 20th ranked defense. Marginally worse than the Browns are this week.

Will Caley have a running game or rely solely on Stroud again? Will the defense continue their return to 2025 form or backslide? How these things play out will certainly impact the Monday mood.

Which takes us back to the opening question: are the Texans ascending or pretending? From the looks of things, we’re climbing the hill. Hopefully we’ll still feel that way come Monday morning.

#GoTexans

item.title: Our Defense vs. Their Offense: Carolina Panthers
item.description: The Saints defense can elevate this team to the number 1 spot in the NFC South as they take on the Panthers
item.content:encoded:
In what is an unconventional matchup for the top spot in the division, the 3-5 Saints will host the 3-5 Panthers on Sunday at noon in the Superdome. The Panthers came out hot to start the season, and it looked like head coach Dave Canales had finally figured out how to get the team to progress around QB Bryce Young. The Panthers were, at one point, 3-2 and sitting in the top spot of the NFC South, and Bryce Young was playing the best football of his NFL career. Since then, the Panthers have lost three straight games, including a blowout loss to the Bucs.

The Panthers have still made strides offensively, even though they have been on this losing streak. Currently, the Panthers have the fourth-best passing offense in the NFL, averaging over 261 yards per game. Through the first eight games of the season, Young has thrown for 2,197 yards, 16 TDs, and six INTs. Right now, Young is on pace to finish the season with over 4,500 yards and 34 TDs. Overall, the Panthers are ninth in the NFL in total offense, averaging 362 yards per game, and 11th in scoring, averaging 24.9 points per game.

None of these categories are favorable to the Saints’ defense, as they are currently allowing 370.5 total yards per game, 27 points per game, 236 passing yards per game, and 133.9 rushing yards per game, ranking 27th or worse in the NFL in each category.

The Panthers have the advantage in both rushing and passing, and they have a true No. 1 receiving threat in Tetairoa McMillan. McMillan has recorded 46 receptions for 625 yards and three TDs so far this season. This could present a matchup problem for the Saints’ cornerbacks. The Saints are currently tied for eighth-most in completions of 20-plus yards allowed, having surrendered 28 through eight games. The big-play opportunities are there for opponents, especially considering that not only are those plays available, but there haven’t been many consequences for attempting them, as the Saints have only four INTs on the season.

There are two key areas the Saints can attack. The Carolina offense has been awful at the line of scrimmage when it comes to protecting the QB. The Panthers’ offense has allowed 26 sacks so far this year, averaging 3.25 sacks allowed per game. They have also allowed 104 pressures this year, which is roughly 13 pressures per game.

The Saints have the best pass-rushing duo in the NFL in Chase Young and Carl Granderson. The issue with the Saints’ pass rush is that their pressure rate is still a little low, considering how dominant that pair of edge rushers has been. The Saints currently rank just 26th in the league in pressure rate, which means that if it’s not Young or Granderson, the pressure isn’t consistently getting through. Given how poorly the Panthers’ offensive line has performed in pass protection, this game should help improve that number.

The other area where the Saints could win is on third down. The Saints are allowing opponents to convert 47.2% of their third-down attempts, but the Panthers are only converting 37.7% of their own third-down attempts.

The Saints’ defense will have opportunities to make an impact on this game. They will need to stop the run, contain Bryce Young, and generate pressure with four rushers. If the defense is able to do this, they should be able to limit explosive plays and potentially create turnovers. The Panthers’ offense has given the ball away 12 times this season, and if the Saints can add to that total, they should be able to defend the Dome.

How do you feel about this matchup with the Panthers, and do you think the Saints are rounding into a first-place team?

Share your thoughts in the comments.

item.title: Panthers vs Saints: How injuries will dictate this week’s storylines
item.description: Breaking down the biggest stories going into this weeks game!
item.content:encoded:
Hello CSR! We’re on to another game week, which means we can look forward to another game of football to hopefully wipe the slate clean and get Carolina moving in the right direction again. This week, the Panthers will travel to New Orleans to face my personal most hated division rival, the New Orleans Saints. What better way to bounce back from a loss against Sean Payton’s Broncos than defeating his former team? That math maths, right?

The Panthers designated RB Jonathon Brooks, WR Xavier Legette, and CB Mike Jackson to return from injured/reserve this week, joining OL Brady Christensen whom they designated to return last week. So the Panthers appear to be finally getting reinforcements soon, which is why I decided to devote this week’s Storylines piece to the Panthers current injury situation on both sides of the ball. The team may not get any of those 4 guys back for this week, that will be dictated by how their practices go over the coming days and how the medical staff evaluates them. So let’s take a look at their current situations on offense and defense.

Offense: The Offensive Line is getting healthier, but can they bounce back?

On top of the aforementioned Brooks, Christensen, and Legette, OG Damien Lewis practiced in full on Wednesday. He has been the Panthers best offensive linemen when healthy this season, and his presence has been sorely missed. So depending on what happens with Brady Christensen, the Panthers could have two key offensive linemen returning this week. But honestly, the Panthers offensive line wasn’t as bad this past weekend as they have been previously, but they still allowed pressure and sacks leading to turnovers in very key situations. This week, they draw a Saints defense that isn’t the best as far as yardage per game is concerned, but they can pressure the passer. And in recent history, this defense has given Carolina’s offense fits. Of all games to right the trend of losses against New Orleans, this is the week, as Carolina still sits at number one in the NFC South despite their recent string of losses. They need to keep Bryce Young upright to take advantage of the Saints bottom third of the league defense in most statistical categories.

Defense: The secondary again a storyline

I’m not expecting Mike Jackson to return this week, but him being activated gives the Panthers about 3 weeks to evaluate him and decide if he’s healthy. But, there’s more good news in the secondary as Will Lee III managed a full practice on Wednesday. In addition, the Panthers finally activated Corey Thornton on Sunday, and he managed a really nice interception as the Panthers defense had a relatively okay game. I imagine Marco Wilson might get the call up once again for this secondary as well. They’ll have their work cut out for them, as the Saints have Chris Olave and now first round picks Jordyn Tyson getting more snaps coming off his injuries in the off-season. They’ll need to try their best to match up against these guys without Mike Jack and Jaycee Horn.

Bonus Storyline: Looks like they’ll get Jaelan Phillips back

The Panthers have spent the last few weeks without their big 2026 free agency signing Jaelan Phillips, which has greatly impacted their pass rush and the setting of the edge in the run game. He appears to be back this week after practicing in full on Wednesday coming off a hamstring injury. Its not a guarantee he will return, as those hammy injuries can pop back up, but at this juncture its promising. Which, having him return will help a defense that might be missing LB Bobby Okereke, who is still nursing the same foot injury that kept him out last week.

What storylines are you watching this week, Panthers fans?

item.title: Seahawks defense presents a major test for Fernando Mendoza’s first NFL start
item.description: Mendoza gets his first NFL start against Seattle, where Macdonald’s defense has made life difficult for rookie QBs.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks’ next opponent is making a major change at quarterback. After trading Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings, the Las Vegas Raiders are turning to Fernando Mendoza, the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, as their starter for Week 10.

Mendoza has already made his NFL debut, completing six of eight passes for 48 yards in garbage time against the New England Patriots. Sunday, however, will be a different challenge: his first career start against the reigning Super Bowl champions and one of the NFL’s most difficult defenses to prepare for.

The Cousins trade also has implications beyond Las Vegas. Minnesota is strengthening its quarterback room with a familiar veteran, potentially improving the offense of a team competing in the same NFC playoff picture as Seattle. While the Vikings still have questions to answer, the move makes them a team worth watching in the wild-card race.

For the Seahawks, though, the immediate focus is Mendoza. And if history is any indication, Mike Macdonald has a particularly uncomfortable welcome waiting for the rookie.

A difficult matchup for first-year quarterbacks

Macdonald has built his defensive reputation around disguise, pressure and forcing opposing quarterbacks to make decisions before they are entirely comfortable with what they see. That combination can be especially difficult for a rookie. Young quarterbacks are still learning how quickly NFL defenses close throwing windows, how protections should respond to different fronts and when a seemingly open receiver is actually being baited into a dangerous throw.

Macdonald frequently uses simulated pressures and disguised coverages to complicate those decisions. A defense can show a threatening blitz before dropping defenders into coverage, or present what looks like a manageable protection before sending pressure from an unexpected angle.

The objective is not just sending more rushers; it is to make the quarterback unsure of where the pressure is coming from and which areas of the field will remain open after the snap. That uncertainty creates two opportunities for Seattle.

The first is hesitation: if the quarterback holds the ball while identifying the rush, the pass rush gets more time to reach him. The second is a rushed decision: if he anticipates pressure and throws early, he may deliver the ball into a coverage that looks different from the one he initially read.

For an experienced quarterback, these situations are challenging enough. For a rookie making his first start, the margin for error is considerably smaller.

The numbers against rookie quarterbacks

Seattle’s recent matchups with rookie starters illustrate the challenge.

Across the four games against Bo Nix, Caleb Williams, Cam Ward, and Max Brosmer, the quarterbacks combined for 642 passing yards, seven interceptions and 17 sacks. Those quarterbacks completed 89 of 142 pass attempts, for a combined completion percentage of 62.7%.

The most striking numbers are the sacks and interceptions. Seattle averaged more than four sacks and nearly two interceptions per game in this sample. That is a demanding combination for any offense, especially one relying on a quarterback who has not yet experienced the full speed and complexity of an NFL defense as a starter.

The passing-yardage average also tells part of the story. Although Cam Ward threw for 256 yards, the other three quarterbacks combined for just 386. The overall average was 160.5 yards per game, with the individual performances varying considerably.

The results were equally notable: Seattle won all four games.

Four games, four different challenges

Bo Nix opened his rookie season against Seattle in September 2024. The Seahawks held him to 138 passing yards, intercepted him twice and sacked him twice in a 26–20 victory. Nix completed 26 of 42 attempts, but the volume did not translate into an efficient passing performance.

Caleb Williams had an even more difficult afternoon. In a 6–3 Seahawks win, he completed 16 of 28 passes for 122 yards, threw an interception and was sacked seven times. The game demonstrated how a defense can disrupt an offense without needing to generate a large number of points itself.

Cam Ward provided a different test in 2025. He completed 28 of 42 passes for 256 yards without an interception, but Seattle still recorded four sacks and won 30–24. His production showed that rookie quarterbacks can find opportunities against this defense, even when the overall matchup remains difficult.

Max Brosmer’s experience was the most punishing statistically. In Seattle’s 26–0 shutout of Minnesota, he completed 19 of 30 passes for 126 yards, threw four interceptions (including an awful pick-six to Ernest JOnes) and took four sacks.

The four games offer different lessons. Nix struggled with turnovers, Williams was overwhelmed by pressure, Ward produced yards but could not lead Tennessee to victory, and Brosmer endured a disastrous afternoon against a defense that consistently won the decisive plays.

Mendoza will need to avoid all four outcomes.

What this means for Fernando Mendoza

Mendoza enters the matchup with an impressive college résumé, including a Heisman Trophy and a national championship at Indiana. But college accomplishments cannot eliminate the learning curve involved in facing an NFL defense.

His most important task may not be producing explosive plays. It may be avoiding the mistakes that allow Seattle to control the game.

That means getting the protection calls right, identifying where pressure could come from, trusting the answers built into the offensive scheme and knowing when an incompletion is preferable to forcing a throw. The Raiders will also need to help him with a credible running game and manageable third downs.

If Mendoza repeatedly has to hold the ball while deciphering Seattle’s coverage, the Seahawks’ pass rush could take over. If he anticipates pressure and throws without confirming the post-snap picture, Macdonald’s disguises could create turnover opportunities.

The Raiders cannot expect their rookie to solve every problem on his own. The coaching staff must put him in positions where he can make quick, defined reads rather than asking him to consistently win complicated passing situations.

For Seattle, the plan is straightforward: make the rookie prove he can recognize the defense, protect the football and respond when the first option is unavailable.

Final Thoughts

Fernando Mendoza’s first NFL start presents the Seahawks with an opportunity to test a rookie against a defense built to create uncertainty. Macdonald’s system does not rely exclusively on overwhelming quarterbacks with blitzes; it combines pressure with disguise, forcing passers to diagnose the play while the pocket is already changing around them.

Seattle’s recent results against rookie starters are encouraging. Those numbers do not guarantee another dominant performance, but they establish a clear challenge for Las Vegas.

For the Seahawks, the ideal outcome is to make the rookie hesitate, force him into difficult decisions and turn those moments into sacks, turnovers and stalled drives. If Seattle executes that plan, Mendoza could discover just how steep the learning curve can be when facing Mike Macdonald’s defense for the first time as a starter.

item.title: Patrick Mahomes doesn’t expect a long learning period for Josh Downs
item.description: Kansas City’s quarterback says his newest wideout’s body of work speaks for itself.
item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday, the Kansas City Chiefs executed a trade with the Indianapolis Colts to bring in wide receiver Josh Downs in return for a pair of Day 3 draft selections.

Now that the move is official, the process of integrating Downs into the offense begins. Speaking before Wednesday’s practice, quarterback Patrick Mahomes did not foresee a problem.

Mahomes expects his new target to be on the field as he learns Kansas City’s offense.

“It is realistic,” Mahomes explained, “because we do a great job of kind of moving guys in and out of every single position, and so guys know the entire concepts of the plays. We’re very detailed with how we call the plays in the huddle, which will help him out a ton. Then when he doesn’t know, being able to talk to me in the huddle or talk to the guys as they’re breaking the huddle, and that usually helps when the guys like each other.

“It’s good to have a guy that you can tell everybody’s going to like and that he has his head on the right way and he’s going to make sure that he’s going to do whatever it takes to win.”

Mahomes has no question about what Downs brings to the Chiefs.

“He does a great job of winning one-on-one matchups,” observed Mahomes, “which is always important. He runs routes really well. He sets them up really well, where he will run a route early in the game that he sets up for another one later in the game.

“Then he has really good feel,” Mahomes said. “Obviously, playing in the system that he has — he has a lot of read-type routes, and you can tell he knows how to get himself open, settle in the right zones, and win versus man when he can. So, I think it will be an easy transition for him to kind of do that stuff in our offense. Then with how we do things, he can play a lot of different positions as we move receivers and tight ends around.”

Speaking after Mahomes, Downs explained the obvious answer to how he will work himself into the system.

“When [Mahomes] throws me the ball, just catch it,” he remarked, “and keep making plays when he throws it to me and do anything I can to learn the offense as fast as possible.

“I don’t want to be a guy that’s asking everybody what the play is or what the formation is,” Downs pointed out. “I feel like that’s when you kind of get left behind. So, I want to do everything I can to learn as fast as possible.”

Mahomes elaborated on the learning ahead of Downs, who he believes is up for the challenge after seeing his attention in Wednesday’s walk through.

“The entire offense will probably take a couple weeks,” he predicted, “but I think what I’ve learned just from meeting Josh is he’s very intelligent. He has a good feel for playing in the NFL, and their scheme is similar to our scheme. Obviously, verbiage and everything like that, but we can utilize him in his role in his spots. At the end of the day, when you get guys in the building, and they’re picking up stuff like we were at walkthrough earlier and he’s picking up stuff quickly, then you can kind of give him more and more. And so, he’s definitely a smart football player, and I think it won’t be a long time until he’s really getting utilized in the offense.”

One of Downs’ new teammates believes the adjustment will be easier than expected.

“It’s not really hard to understand what Pat’s thinking on the field,” wideout Rashee Rice declared on Wednesday. “Once you love the game of football and you’re doing everything you can to get open, Pat’s going to do everything he can to get you the ball. So, as long as you separate and make some room to make sure he can make the throw, which he will. So, as long as he does that, it’ll be easy for him to prepare for the plays.”

Other recent wide receiver trades for the Chiefs — such Kadarius Toney and DeAndre Hopkins — ultimately underwhelmed despite flashy moments. Neither was in Downs’ position, and he has proven himself while still playing for a second contract.

“He’s done it,” Mahomes reiterated of Downs. “You can see that he’s made plays against some of the best defenses in the league and teams that we’ll go up against this season and in the playoffs. Whenever he’s put that on tape, then you know that that is there and so now it’s about us utilizing his skillset within the other guys on the team in order to make the offense even better than we’ve been so far.”

item.title: 3 reasons why the Bengals will beat the Steelers on SNF, and 3 reasons they won’t
item.description: Hopefully the Bengals walk out of Sunday Night Football with a 7-2 record and the lead in the division.
item.content:encoded:
It’s Week 10, which means we’re halfway through the season. The playoff picture is starting to come into view, and the Cincinnati Bengals are 6-2 with a chance to take a firm grasp of the AFC North. They host the Pittsburgh Steelers, also 6-2, who beat the Bengals in Pittsburgh in Week 3, 30-27.

The game will be in front of a national audience on Sunday Night Football under the lights, and the Bengals will wear their “White Bengal” uniform. With the history between these two teams and what’s at stake, this is one of the biggest games played at Paycor Stadium in the last few years.

Here are three reasons why the Bengals will beat the Steelers in front of a home crowd on Sunday night (followed by three reasons why they won’t).

Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins

That’s reason No. 1.

Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins make up the best quarterback-wide receiver trio in the NFL, and it’s not even close. Burrow and Chase have played football together for the better part of a decade, and Higgins and Burrow have been together their entire NFL careers.

And they complement each other perfectly.

Chase is a generational talent. He can play on the outside or in the slot or out of the backfield. He can run any route, and he can burn about any defensive back in a footrace. On top of that, when he gets the ball in his hands, he turns into a running back—capable of breaking tackles and turning a five-yard reception into a 60-yard touchdown any time he touches the ball.

Tee is a big-bodied receiver—6-foot-4, 220 pounds—but he too can fly. His greatest strength, though, is his literal strength when it comes to catching the ball in traffic. You could make a two-hour movie out of his highlights when it comes to keeping the ball in his hands and defensive backs are draped all over him.

The only reason Higgins isn’t WR1 is that Chase is Chase.

Bengals Defensive Line

The defense is improved. It’s not perfect, but it is better. What makes it better is the defensive line. The Bengals went all in on that one position group.

They traded the No. 10 overall pick for Dexter Lawrence, who has been a dominant force in the middle all season long. They also signed Jonathan Allen, who has played extremely well next to Lawrence, and Boye Mafe, who ranks among PFF’s top pass rushers so far this season.

On top of the free agent additions, they retained last year’s starters, BJ Hill and TJ Slaton, as well as their 2024 second-round pick, Kris Jenkins Jr. Sprinkle in Myles Murphy, Cedric Johnson, and possibly Shemar Stewart (I know, I know…), and the Bengals have one of the deepest defensive lines in the league.

So at the end of the game, when the Steelers’ offensive line is sucking wind, and Aaron Rodgers needs time to find his ogre of a tight end for a first down, maybe they won’t be able to hold off a Lawrence who has just taken a couple plays off on the sideline to catch his breath.

Week 10 Offense > Week 3 Offense

We’ve seen this story before.

The Bengals, though they started the season 2-0, looked weird doing it on offense. They were still in offseason mode, like Burrow and the rest of his offense typically are until late October.

Now, the offense is firing on all cylinders. Burrow has thrown for over 1,200 yards, 16 touchdowns, and only three interceptions. If he continues this trend, it would be hard to deny him the MVP.

So, if you go back and watch the Bengals lose to the Steelers in Week 3, and then you watch their offense over the last four weeks, you’ll notice they look much better now.

Bonus Reason: You

This game has potential to be insane. The two teams don’t like each other already, and with what’s at stake, the stadium is going to be LOUD.

I’d like to see Rodgers communicate a change to his receivers and offensive line when he can’t even hear himself think.

So be loud.

————————————————————————————————————————————

And now, unfortunately, three reasons why the Bengals won’t win on Sunday:

The Bengals’ Secondary

If the Bengals have a big weakness, it’s their secondary. The front office didn’t address the cornerback position despite the overall lack of quality depth, and now it could come back to bite them.

The Steelers don’t boast a receiving corps nearly as good as the Bengals’, but there’s talent there, and Rodgers has spent an entire career making receivers look good.

At 42 years old, Rodgers is playing at a high level, and if the Bengals let him run around in the backfield and avoid pressure the way he did in Week 3 again, he will find open receivers and move the ball down the field. The Bengals’ secondary isn’t good enough to lock up receivers for an extended period of time, and Rodgers is perfectly capable of carving them up if he gets the opportunity to do so.

Jaylen Warren

Rodgers might be the star on the Steelers’ offense, but Warren has been incredible for Pittsburgh. He’s averaging 5.9 yards per carry, which leads the league among running backs with a lot of carries. He averages 88 yards per game, which is more than the Bengals’ offense averages. He’s PFF’s highest-graded running back, and he has more yards and averages more yards after contact per attempt than any other running back in the league with a minimum of 50% of the carries.

Lawrence might be really good at stopping the run when the offense tries to run between the tackles, but he can’t be everywhere. And one major weakness of the Bengals’ defense is their ability to stop the run on the outside.

One of the best ways for the Steelers to defend against Burrow is to keep him on the sidelines, and one of the best ways to keep him on the sidelines is to let Warren carry the ball and chew clock.

The Steelers are coming off a bye; the Bengals are coming off an international game

This matters.

The Steelers are fully rested and are coming off their bye week. They haven’t played a football game since Nov. 1 and are relatively healthy.

The Bengals, on the other hand, not only played on Nov. 8, but they played that game in Madrid, Spain. Then they had to fly back across the planet to Cincinnati and pretend like everything’s normal. They do get the benefit of waiting to play football until Sunday night, but if the NFL wants to continue their international games, they’re going to have to think about giving teams an extra bye week before they have to travel that far.

The Bengals had a good trip, but the stress and adjustment to different time zones probably made things a little more difficult than they would have been had they played the Falcons in Atlanta.

What do you think will happen on Sunday night?

item.title: Source: Daiyan Henley failed Broncos physical
item.description: Knee issue caused Denver to scrap trade with Chargers.
item.content:encoded:
When word emerged that the trade that would have sent linebacker Daiyan Henley from the Chargers to the Broncos was called off, no specific details were provided. Common sense pointed to a failed physical and, for a change, common sense was accurate.

Per a source with knowledge of the situation, Henley did indeed fail the physical in Denver.

It was, we're told, a knee issue. Although Henley appeared on the Week 9 injury report with a shoulder problem, he was listed with a knee injury in Week 6.

Every trade hinges on the passing of a physical. The player rarely fails it. Still, when he does, the trade doesn't happen.

The problem with eleventh-hour deadline deals that fall through is that the team that thought it was acquiring a new player now can't pivot elsewhere.

Of course, there's always the possibility that the Broncos got cold feet after committing a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick to the transaction. As everyone learned with the failed Maxx Crosby trade from the Raiders to the Ravens, the standards can shift from team to team.

Crosby, who stayed with the Raiders, has started all nine games — and he has been on the field for 89 percent of the snaps. Henley, who has started all eight Chargers games and played 87 percent of the snaps, presumably will return to action for the Chargers.

Early Thursday morning, roughly 36 hours after the NFL’s trade deadline, multiple NFL insiders reported that the Chargers’ deal with the Broncos that sent linebacker Daiyan Henley to Denver in exchange for two draft picks has fallen through and will be withdrawn. The Bolts were set to receive a 2027 fourth-rounder and a 2028 fifth-round pick in return.

The reason for the nixed trade was not immediately given, but it’s presumed to be due to a failed physical after he Broncos discovered an issue in one of Henley’s knees.

Following the breaking of the news, Henley took to social media and dropped a .gif of a person looking extremely confused, possibly pointing to his own confusion about why he would have failed his physical (if that was truly the case here). Henley was limited to begin Texans week but would go on to be a full participant both Thursday and Friday before being completely taken off the final injury report.

Either way, the Chargers keep their team captain and will now go without two extra early day three picks over the next two drafts.

item.title: Week 10 FLEX Finder: Target vacuums for Rams, Colts, Cardinals
item.description: Rivers McCown offers running backs, wideouts, and tight ends he thinks can outperform low expectations in Week 10.
item.content:encoded:
The trade deadline has come and gone, but it is good ol' fashioned injuries that have created most of this article. Puka Nacua, Rhamondre Stevenson, Jaylin Noel and Michael Wilson have left plenty of volume on the table for their backups and, in one case, returning stars. The only major fantasy football players that changed teams were the Colts receivers Josh Downs and Keenan Allen, leaving a nice little floating pair of question marks over their entire offense.

Rules for this weekly article:

1) I will not recommend quarterbacks — There are plenty of good ones. You’re on your own there.
2) I will not recommend any running back who costs more than $5,000, wideout who costs more than $4,500, or tight end that costs more than $4,000 in DraftKings’ DFS slate — This was an easy cutoff for what a FLEX really is.
3) I consider any player who garners over 50 yards or scores a victory for the column — anything more you get out of that, well, great for you. Let’s set expectations low because we are combing for outliers.

Nico Collins, Darren Waller headline Week 10’s Regression Files
Denny Carter breaks down which players might be due for positive or negative regression headed into Week 10
  • Denny Carter,

▶ Running Backs

Omarion Hampton, LAC -- $4,900 – I don’t exactly love Hampton’s role, and the fact that he’s fallen far enough to be in this column is a dark sign. Still, the Ravens are starting Jacoby Brissett, and Hampton is coming off a 13/60 game against the Texans. The Ravens don’t have an extraordinary run defense. I don’t love the play, but it feels like one of the safer FLEX spots of the week.

Corey Kiner, NE -- $4,700 – With Rhamondre Stevenson lost to a knee injury and TreVeyon Henderson dealing with a terrifying-sounding neurological problem, Kiner is suddenly next man up for the Patriots in a game with a 50.5 over/under overseas against the Lions. Kiner had already begun to butt in on carries, and my guess is he’ll get the bulk of the work here.

Audric Estime, NO -- $4,500 – Please disregard this pick if Travis Etienne manages to play this week off injured reserve, but I like Estime’s odds of continuing to hog carries alongside Alvin Kamara. The Panthers have demonstrated this year that they are capable of getting absolutely torched in the run game, and their lack of healthy good cornerbacks leaves them stuck in passive coverages and box structures.

Emmett Johnson, KC -- $4,700 – Trading for Josh Downs should help the Chiefs pass catchers have a better floor than they’ve had most of the season, but the NFL does not often provide one-week integration plans for non-quarterbacks. Johnson has now scored in back-to-back games and will also get a small share of the Kenneth Walker workload, while the reeling Falcons do not exactly qualify as a scary test as the Chiefs are road favorites.

Moves to Make Before Week 10 Fantasy Football: Buy Ollie Gordon, sell Drake London
Ollie Gordon and Drake London headline the players to buy or sell in fantasy football trades before Week 10 of the NFL season.
  • Alfredo Brown,

▶ Wide receivers

Konata Mumpfield, LAR -- $4,000 – In the wake of Puka Nacua’s knee injury, we must ask ourselves questions such as “Which Rams receivers are still alive?” and “Do we really want to know the answer to this question?” Since they won’t let us unretire Az-Zahir Hakim, we feel compelled to note that Mumpfield looks likely to benefit from Nacua’s injury.

Tank Dell, HOU -- $3,900 – Texans receivers' snap counts are important things to keep in mind, but the targets are what we want. Dell had nine and was always a favorite C.J. Stroud target before his devastating knee injury. I don’t necessarily want to say that I’m happy his snap count is low, but I do think it’s been a bit overblown. Dell looks good even if he and Stroud are still working on some timing. The Texans pass offense looks good. The Texans running game is theoretical. Don’t expect WR1 stuff, but WR3 is in the range of possibilities.

Savion Williams, GB -- $3,900 – I know this is a weird spot to pick on given the Vikings defense, but the Packers pass offense absolutely has proven they can dunk on anyone – they even did officially dunk on the Vikings defense in Week 1 – and you know there will be downfield shots. I’d love to see Williams used more in that area, but the screen game is another important constraint against Minnesota’s blitzing style and I expect the targets to keep coming after last week’s touchdown. No Josh Jacobs could further tilt targets towards the gadget player as well.

Ashton Dulin, IND -- $3,100 – If you want to feel disgusting – and I mean absolutely disgusting – look at the Colts wideout room right now after Josh Downs and Keenan Allen were dispatched to other areas of the globe. Someone, believe it or not, will be required to catch the ball against the Dolphins. Tyler Warren can’t have all the targets. Dulin was the offseason WR3 and broke a 55-yard touchdown on a screen against the Cowboys last week. The Dolphins will be starting Kyle McCord at quarterback. It’s a free country and you can do what you want, but someone must catch the ball for the Colts in a game they are favored to win.

Reggie Virgil, ARI -- $3,400 – Another documented case of “someone here has to catch a football.” Virgil was the only non-Trey McBride Cardinals receiver who is still healthy that had more than two targets last week. Simi Fehoko figures to be the other starting outside receiver, Devin Duvernay has been a punt returner for the better part of a decade now, and Harrison Wallace III is a 23-year-old UDFA who was waived at last cuts and saw no takers. The practice squad is full of potential elevations, but most of them are names that haven’t been relevant in a long time. (Phillip Dorsett still being around is incredible.) The Rams will speed up Carson Beck’s clock and try to do what they can to take away McBride. These are all reasons to believe someone will do something here. And for all we know, maybe Virgil is that person.

▶ Tight ends

Chig Okonkwo, WAS -- $3,800 – We haven’t exactly seen The Chigassance hit yet, but 6/56 against the Rams was a good look for the highly-paid free-agent signing and he’s certainly been more involved than Antonio Williams so far after Terry McLaurin’s injury. The Giants allow 8.5 passes to tight ends per game, a top-10 rate in the league, per FTN’s numbers.

Darnell Washington, PIT -- $3,200 – The Bengals continue to be the cure for the common tight end line and the two Steelers tight ends combined for 97 yards against them in Week 3. With it feeling like the Steelers are generally looking Washington’s way come end zone time, I think he’s probably the play over the more reliable Pat Freiermuth, though both could ultimately get there.

item.title: Bengals sent Zac Taylor to clear the Eagles’ name in failed Arnold Ebiketie trade
item.description: The Bengals GM sent a message via Zac Taylor absolving the Eagles from blame of the Arnold Ebiketie trade falling apart.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles and Bengals thought they had a deal in place to send Arnold Ebiketie from Philadelphia to Cincinnati, but just an hour after the trade was announced, it had reportedly been canceled. Insiders like Adam Schefter were quick to report that the trade falling apart was not due to a physical or performance concern, and it was eventually revealed to be a miscalculation on what Ebiketie would cost the team.

Initial trade terms was sending a sixth-round draft pick to the Eagles in exchange for the OLB, but since Ebiketie was a compensatory free agent, trading for him would negate the Bengals future third-round comp pick from the Trey Hendrickson trade. Adding in the loss of a third-rounder, in addition to the agreed upon sixth-round pick, made the trade to expensive for Cincinnati, so they bailed on the deal.

Instead of speaking to reporters about the incident himself, Bengals GM Duke Tobin sent a message via head coach Zac Taylor about the situation — who admitted he didn’t really feel comfortable with the specific way Tobin wanted things portrayed —, but wanted it to be clear that Howie Roseman and the Eagles were good trade partners.

Mike Garafolo said that the vibes inside the Eagles building were very angry, and how teams move in these situations can absolutely affect future trades and team’s willingness to do business together. Taylor shouldn’t have been the messenger, but it was important for Tobin to clear the air and make sure this move wouldn’t even further affect the Eagles in a negative way.

The Daily Slop – 12 November 2026

Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Commanders links

Articles

The Athletic (paywall)

Why Commanders fans should still be pulling for a turnaround under Dan Quinn

The thing about firing Dan Quinn as coach of the Washington Commanders — though it would placate an increasingly dissatisfied fanbase — is there’s a trickledown that would leave the franchise in a state that has defined it for far too long: unstable.

Bear with me, because a vote for the status quo could seem — how to put this? — wild at the moment. This isn’t a case that Quinn should keep his job based on his team’s current trajectory as much as it is a warning about what would follow if the losses continue.

When things are going as they are — and Washington is 4-15-1 over the last 13 months — people tend to want heads to roll. Change becomes the only way to satisfy that. It’s an emotional response, which is fine, because what’s the point in rooting for a sports franchise if it doesn’t manage to tap into your emotions?

But think about the fallout if Quinn and his staff don’t survive. Their fate hangs in the remaining results, which must start improving beginning Thursday night against the New York Giants at the Meadowlands. There are a host of reasons any Commanders fan who is interested in the long-term stability and success of the franchise should root for a turnaround.

[Josh Harris’s] record in the other two American sports franchises he owns would suggest Harris isn’t afraid of change. That’s good. A willingness to admit mistakes should be a trait of a good owner.

But if Quinn is ousted after his third season, wouldn’t the start to Harris’ stewardship feel — and it’s scary to go here — a little Snyder-esque?

The way to avoid that: Have Quinn and his crew turn this season around. At this point, that might seem unlikely, but in the interest of distancing this franchise from the previous quarter-century, it would be the best outcome for everyone — from the quarterback to the fans.

Jayden Daniels and J.J. McCarthy Are Trending in Different Directions

On Daniels’s side of the ball, they promoted David Blough to become their new OC and implement a more traditional, under-center style of offense—a significant change after primarily running a no-huddle, shotgun offense under Kliff Kingsbury. They also made numerous roster changes, primarily on the defensive side of the ball as they looked to improve one of the worst-ranked defenses in the NFL during the 2025 campaign.

The new offense has brought mixed results. There are times that Daniels and the offense are in rhythm, such as in the first half of their game against the Rams, when they got out to a 10–6 halftime lead. At other times, they struggle to move the ball at all, such as in the second half or their loss to the Rams, when they couldn’t muster a single first down in the third quarter.

The Commanders’ offense ranks 20th in yards per game (325.4) and passing yards per game (207.4), 21st in points per game (21) and 22nd in EPA per play (-0.08). While McCarthy has changed teams and other quarterbacks from the class saw their teams undergo coaching changes early on (Michael Penix Jr., Caleb Williams and Drake Maye), Daniels could be facing that fate in Year 4 if the Commanders move on from Quinn.

The Commanders have their quarterback in Daniels, but with low playoff hopes (a win Thursday would draw them to two games behind the Giants in the NFC East, while the wild-card field is crowded) and a franchise still figuring out how to properly build around him, his career is at an odd standstill. item.title: Should the Titans re-sign Tony Pollard after declining to trade him?
item.description: The Tennessee Titans did not trade Tony Pollard at the trade deadline; should they re-sign him after this year?
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans were very active leading up to the NFL trade deadline. They traded Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears, and Amani Hooker to the Buffalo Bills. By doing so, Mike Borgonzi acquired four total picks, including two first-rounders for Simmons, and an additional second-rounder for Hooker.

One player who was not traded was running back Tony Pollard. Reports had consistently indicated the Titans preferred to hold onto Pollard because he’s been helping with the development and evaluation of Cam Ward. Regardless of how that makes you feel, it seems those reports were accurate.

Pollard is in a contract year. It was previous GM Ran Carthon who signed the former Memphis standout to a three-year, $21.7 million contract prior to the 2024 campaign. Pollard is currently the 22nd-highest paid back in the league, proving that contract has aged well.

But declining opportunities to trade a 29-year-old RB on an expiring contract when you’re rebuilding the roster is an interesting tactic. It makes us wonder if Borgonzi is considering re-signing Pollard. He’s due for unrestricted free agency.

The running back market has been reset by recent deals for Bijan Robinson, Jahmyr Gibbs, and Saquon Barkley. They are among four RBs earning more than $20 million annually (alongside Jonathan Taylor). Pollard obviously isn’t that tier of back, but the increases in pay will impact his negotiations, too.

Given Pollard’s age, the Titans shouldn’t re-sign him to longer than a two-year extension. Given his advancing age, they’ll want to protect themselves against overpaying for a declining talent. Signing Pollard to a two-year, $20 million contract feels fair.

Pollard would earn $10 million annually, making him the 16th-highest paid back in the NFL right behind Kyren Williams ($11m AAV). Other happenings around the league might impact this, but that feels like the appropriate range for a Pollard extension.

item.title: 3 things to watch in 49ers-Cowboys: Run the football, Kyle
item.description: 40 carries have to be the goal again on Sunday
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys will meet on Sunday and continue a storied history between the two franchises. What was once a rivalry has turned into an avalanche, with the 49ers’ winning streak over the Cowboys spanning several years. Sunday is expected to be a high-scoring affair with two high-powered offenses, and Vegas believes it too, with the highest implied total of the weekend.

Former pass game coordinator and defensive backs coach for the Philadelphia Eagles under Vic Fangio, Christian Parker took over as defensive coordinator for Dallas this season, and let’s just say things have not gone well. Kyle Shanahan and the 49ers know starting linebacker Dee Winters very well also. You can bet Shanahan and Brock Purdy will have the Cowboys’ linebackers in a bind constantly on Sunday.

What else will the 49ers look to exploit on Sunday? Here are three things to watch for Sunday.

The 49ers’ rushing attack

It may not feel like it, but the 49ers’ rushing attack is number one in several reliable metrics. Not only are the 49ers number one in EPA/play (0.14), success rate (52.1%), and total EPA (66.26; Buffalo is second at 53.09), but they also lead in EPA/ rush, with Buffalo at 0.05 and a league-high success rate on the ground of 50.4%.

Dallas’ defense ranks 27th in the NFL with an EPA/rush allowed of -0.02 and 25th in success rate allowed on the ground at 43.2%. After facing the worst run defense in the league in total rushing yards allowed last week, the 49ers face the second-worst run defense in Dallas with 1,327 rushing yards allowed and 4.99 rushing yards per attempt.

Even pushing to a heavier box count is unlikely, as Dallas has an 18.1% rate. That number is good for 30th in the NFL. That 40-carry number is in the 49ers’ sights for a second consecutive week.

49ers motion percentage

The 49ers hold a slight edge in motion percentage over the Miami Dolphins at 73.% to Miami’s 73.2% for the league high mark. It’s not just the amount of motion, but the types of motions, which include the often-used banana motions from Kyle Juszczyk. The advantages of the motion in the run game, to change number counts, and in the pass game to help identify coverages are a huge part of the offense.

Dallas is dead last with a 0.11 EPA allowed per play against motion. Good luck, Dallas. The 49ers rank fourth in motion at snap with 50.6%.

Dak Prescott against the 49ers’ preferred coverages

The 49ers are primarily a zone coverage defense, specifically Cover 3. Under Raheem Morris, the 49ers haven’t changed their defensive coverage base much, but there has been an increase in man coverage looks, even if the increase isn’t significant in comparison to zone looks.

Dak Prescott has punished Cover 3 with his third-highest EPA per play of 0.231. On 79 attempts, Prescott averages 7.9 YPA. Against Cover 0, which is a blitz coverage, Prescott struggled mightily with an EPA of -0.276, but he has only 29 attempts. The 49ers failed to pressure Michael Penix in Atlanta, and a similar output won’t go over well against Dallas and their offense.

Nick Bosa and DeForest Buckner must turn up the heat Sunday. Perhaps an Osa Odighizuwa revenge game?

item.title: Commanders at New York Giants 'Thursday Night Football' betting odds, picks and predictions: Best bets, player props
item.description: Our NFL handicapper breaks down his favorite bets in the Commanders-Giants matchup on "Thursday Night Football."
item.content:encoded:
Bright lights will shine down on MetLife Stadium on Thursday, when the New York Giants host the Washington Commanders in a crucial showdown between NFC East rivals.

The Giants enter this meeting with their all-too-familiar foes fresh off a workmanlike, 19-11 road victory over the beleaguered Philadelphia Eagles. Quarterbacks Jameis Winston and J.J. McCarthy combined under center to lead New York (5-2-1) to its second consecutive win.

As for their opponent, this is the most important game of the season for the Commanders. The struggling franchise enters this affair fresh off a 20-13 home loss to the Los Angeles Rams.

It might sound cliche, but if there were ever a must-win situation for Washington (2-5-1), this game is clearly it. A defeat would put the Commanders — 0-3 on the road — four games behind the Giants in the division and deliver a serious blow to their chances of reaching the postseason.

When it comes to the betting market, you can find the Giants favored anywhere from 1.5 points to 2.5 points, depending on the book. As for the total, the number currently ranges from 40.5 to 41.5 points.

With plenty on the line for both teams, let's take a deep dive into this contest and see where we can find some betting value.

Washington Commanders at New York Giants (-2.5, 41.5)

The Giants have a pretty impressive record, but whom have they beaten? I will give New York and its blue-bleeding faithful a checkmark for what I think was a quality road win against the struggling Houston Texans.

Other than that, the Giants have victories against Dallas, Tennessee, Arizona and Philadelphia. The combined record of those teams? An ugly 10-25. Not one of those teams is above .500 in the standings. Throw in Houston, and New York has five victories against teams with a combined 13 wins.

On the flip side, I don't know what to make of the Commanders. They handed Seattle a 33-31 defeat on Sept. 27 at Northwest Stadium. They played the Rams and San Francisco 49ers tight in close defeats. Yet what sticks out are the loss to the Indianapolis Colts and that unforgivable tie against the Giants in their previous meeting.

To sum it up, Washington is mediocrity defined.

When it comes to the respective offenses, they're very much alike. The Commanders rank 11th in rushing yards (118.3 yards per game), while the Giants check in at 17th (112.1 YPG). As for the aerial attacks, they're also similar: New York sits 16th in total passing yards (221 YPG), with Washington not far off in 21st (207 YPG).

I don't trust QB Jayden Daniels and his banged-up offense. And I don't like this team's chances of getting its first win on the road in a prime-time confrontation with an opponent trending upward.

I'm jumping on New York to get the job done against Washington and take a firm grip on the NFC East under first-year head coach John Harbaugh.

Bet: Giants ML (-134, FanDuel)

Player props

WR Malik Nabers – 70+ receiving yards (-104) | 80+ receiving yards (+146) | 90+ receiving yards (+205) | 100+ receiving yards (+300)

Nabers had a relatively subdued showing against Philadelphia, finishing with just five receptions (on eight targets) for 43 yards. However, those paltry stats by his standards were nothing compared to what he did prior to that game.

In his four contests before the clash with the Eagles, Nabers went off:

  • 10/25 at Houston: 7 catches for 111 yards

  • 10/18 vs. New Orleans: 12 catches for 165 yards

  • 10/11 at Washington: 11 catches for 121 yards

  • 10/04 vs. Arizona: 6 catches for 112 yards

Now, he faces that same Washington side against which he was targeted a stunning 20 times in their previous meeting.

I'm taking a swing on Nabers via this ladder play for receiving yards. McCarthy is going to target Nabers plenty throughout the night, giving me optimism the wideout will go off against the Washington secondary again.

LB Arvell Reese to record a sack (+182, FanDuel)

The rookie linebacker, selected fifth overall in this year's NFL Draft, has been so good that he's currently the even-money favorite to earn Defensive Rookie of the Year honors at sportsbooks. The Ohio State product leads the Giants' defense with 68 total tackles (49 solo and 19 assists) and has a team-best 4.5 sacks.

Reese is coming off his most productive game of his young career, finishing with 12 tackles (10 solo) and a whopping 3.0 sacks in last week's road win against Philadelphia.

Now, Reese and the New York defense face a Washington outfit that has been terrible protecting Daniels of late. The Commanders have allowed 15 sacks in their past four contests.

We're getting close to 2-to-1 odds on Arvell getting to Daniels, so I can't pass up this angle tied to a red-hot defender facing a subpar Washington offensive line.

Anytime TD scorers

TE Isaiah Likely (+195, FanDuel)

As a Baltimore Ravens fan, it has been bittersweet watching Likely absolutely light things up for New York.

The New York brass knew what it was doing when it signed the 26-year-old to a three-year, $40 million deal in the offseason. His season résumé – 46 receptions for 448 yards and 6 touchdowns – has put him among the elite at the TE position, and I don't see a decline coming his way.

Just how good are those numbers compared to other tight ends? Likely ranks first in touchdowns, second in targets (66), third in receptions and sixth in receiving yards. Now, he faces a Washington defense allowing just under 70 receiving yards to tight ends (68.8 yards, to be exact), which is fourth-most among NFL defenses.

Earlier this season, Likely put together his best showing against Washington. He finished with 11 catches (on 13 targets) for 94 yards and two touchdowns. The Commanders' defense couldn't stop him then, particularly in the red zone. That same defense is going to have problems containing him in the rematch.

Back Likely to find the end zone at this nice price.

QB J.J. McCarthy (+470, FanDuel)

McCarthy averaged almost 5.0 yards per carry in 10 games last season, finding the end zone on four occasions. Despite a limited sample, the Giants' quarterback has gotten busy with his legs on designed plays or when flushed out of the pocket this campaign, to the tune of nine carries for 51 yards and a 5.7 YPC.

New York running back Cam Skattebo is set to return to the lineup, but I think McCarthy will have a couple of opportunities to get loose on the ground deep in Washington territory and get in the end zone for the first time this season.
